source: Bartra, McGuire, Kable (2013) The valuation system: a coordinate-based meta-analysis of BOLD fMRI experiments
finding: Across fMRI studies, vmPFC and anterior ventral striatum show mostly positive effects of subjective value (SV). These regions look like a domain-general valuation system.
numbers: 206 published fMRI studies. 200 studies report positive SV effects, 77 report negative effects (71 report both). Positive effects in vmPFC and ventral striatum appear at decision and at outcome, and for both monetary and primary rewards.
quote: These regions appear to constitute a "valuation system," carrying a domain-general SV signal
limits: Published coordinates only, so it inherits publication and analysis bias. Reward-vs-penalty contrasts were excluded from one analysis. Overlap of coordinates is not proof of one shared neural code.
agent_relevance: Good support that one scalar value signal exists across reward kinds. Treat common currency as a plausible working model for an agent that compares unlike options, not as settled.

source: Bartra et al. (2013), second finding: mixed-sign regions
finding: Anterior insula, dorsomedial PFC, dorsal and posterior striatum and thalamus show BOTH positive and negative SV effects above chance. This fits a U-shaped arousal or salience signal rather than value.
numbers: Same 206-study corpus. Striatum and insula show a conjunction of positive effects for rewards and negative effects for penalties. Ariely and Berns (2010), cited there: nucleus accumbens activation raised the odds of a reward study by 9:1 (1,351 studies, 68 on reward).
limits: U-shape cannot be separated from value by sign counts alone. Striatal BOLD is not a safe proxy for value, especially when penalties are in the task.
agent_relevance: Salience and value are easy to confuse. An agent that scores options should keep how big and how good as separate quantities.

source: Clithero and Rangel (2014) Informatic parcellation of the network involved in the computation of subjective value
finding: Coordinate meta-analysis of over 80 fMRI papers. vmPFC, ventral striatum and posterior cingulate reliably track value across tasks, reward types and decision/outcome stages.
numbers: 104 parametric subjective-value contrasts overall (global ALE peak 68.89e-3 in left ventral striatum). Decision-value subset N=69 (peak in vmPFC, ALE 63.29e-3). Image-based meta-analysis N=21 contrasts (peak z=6.88 in vmPFC). Thresholds: voxel P<0.001, cluster P<0.05.
limits: Could not include direct cross-modality choices (e.g. movie vs ice cream) because too few exist. Did not separate value from salience. Ventral striatum value effects were absent in some paradigms (cause unknown).
agent_relevance: Convergent with Bartra. Confirms the cross-domain claim for separate evaluations but not for the harder test of direct comparison.

source: Clithero and Rangel (2014), reward-modality gradient
finding: Value is not coded in exactly the same spot for every reward type. There is a posterior-to-anterior gradient in vmPFC from concrete (food) to abstract (money) rewards.
numbers: Direct contrast of money vs food: more food in posterior vmPFC (P<0.005, peak -8,27,-13), more money in anterior vmPFC (P<0.005, peak -5,60,-9). Two co-activation subnetworks inside vmPFC.
limits: Contrasts have limited statistical power. Voxel-level overlap can hide separate neural populations.
agent_relevance: A boundary on one scale: shared region, partly graded content. Abstract goods may need abstraction before comparison.

source: Kable and Glimcher (2007) The neural correlates of subjective value during intertemporal choice
finding: BOLD in ventral striatum, medial PFC and posterior cingulate tracks each person's own discounted value of delayed money. It follows the subjective, not the objective, amount.
numbers: 12 volunteers recruited, 10 scanned. Hyperbolic discounting fit well (median R2 = 0.95, range 0.84-0.98). Discount rate k ranged from 0.0005 to 0.1189. Slope of neural vs behavioral discount rate: VS 0.58 (P=0.04), MPFC 0.75 (P=0.03), PCC 0.80 (P=0.06), all regions 0.69 (P=0.0002). Median neural-minus-behavioral difference near zero.
limits: Tiny sample. One reward type (money) and one task. Value is correlated with close variables (sum, difference or ratio of the two options). Argues against an earlier two-system account (McClure 2004) in this paradigm.
agent_relevance: Shows the method of fitting a person-specific value function and testing it against the brain. Agent analogue: test whether a model's stated value curve matches its choices.

source: Padoa-Schioppa and Assad (2006) Neurons in orbitofrontal cortex encode economic value
finding: In monkey OFC, many neurons encode the value of offered and chosen juices in a way that does not depend on screen position or eye movement. Value is abstract, tied to the good.
numbers: 931 cells recorded, 505 (54%) varied significantly with offer type in at least one time window. Fewer than 5% depended on spatial configuration or motor output. Example session: V(A) = 4.1 V(B) from a sigmoid fit of choices.
limits: One species, juice-for-juice choice. Shows value-like coding, not proof the circuit uses it as a common currency. Critics say value-like tuning can arise from other computations.
agent_relevance: The cleanest picture of choice between goods. Supports separating the evaluation step from the action step in a scaffold.

source: Hayden and Niv (2021) The case against economic values in the orbitofrontal cortex (or anywhere else in the brain)
finding: Argues that cardinal common-currency value may not be computed by default. Value-correlated neurons may reflect other variables, and direct policy learning or heuristics could explain choices without values.
numbers: No new data. Notes that context effects like third-option decoys can be explained by range-normalisation valuation models too (Soltani 2012, Khaw 2017).
quote: economic value, in the cardinal, common-currency sense, is not represented in the brain and used for choice by default
limits: A theoretical case, not an empirical refutation. It accepts that value correlations exist and challenges their interpretation.
agent_relevance: The main rival theory. For an agent, it warns against forcing every choice through an explicit scalar score.

source: The case for value as a common currency in decision-making and intersystem competition (2026 reply to critics)
finding: Defends common currency by refining it: separate decision-phase and learning-phase currencies, options-level and meta-level currencies, mechanistic versus axiomatic versions. Lists three critiques: value-free action paths, dissimilar systems not sharing one currency, and context effects.
numbers: No new data. Cites critique sources: Hayden and Niv 2021, Bennett et al. 2021 (policy-gradient learning in humans), Walasek and Brown 2023, Vlaev 2018.
limits: A conceptual rebuttal. Splitting the claim into versions can make it harder to falsify.
agent_relevance: Clarifies which version is testable. Suggests our agent needs only a decision-phase currency, not a global one.

source: Review (2025) Representation of anticipated rewards and punishments in the human brain
finding: Evidence for common currency comes mostly from positive domains (food, money, goods). Evidence for punishment value is scarce and mixed; some regions encode both valences, others only one.
numbers: No pooled numbers. Cites Kable and Glimcher 2007/2010 (value tracks discounted value, against the two-system view), Levy et al. 2010 (risk and ambiguity share striatal and mPFC value although behaviour was uncorrelated across people), Tom et al. 2007.
limits: Narrative review. Lesion work (Bechara 1994, Fellows and Farah 2007) may reflect broader cognitive deficits rather than value coding.
agent_relevance: Costs and harms may not share the scale with benefits. A scaffold weighing risks against benefits should not assume symmetry.

source: Botvinik-Nezer et al. (2020) Variability in the analysis of a single neuroimaging dataset by many teams (NARPS)
finding: 70 teams analysed the same decision-under-risk fMRI data (gains and losses in vmPFC, ventral striatum, amygdala). Results for the value-system hypotheses differed a lot across teams.
numbers: Data from 108 people (max 54 per hypothesis). Only hypothesis 5 (negative effect of losses in vmPFC) was reported significant by most teams (84.3%). Three hypotheses were significant in 5.7% of teams. Five others (including gain effects in vmPFC and ventral striatum) 21.4% to 37.1%. On average 20% of teams disagreed with the majority. Prediction markets (83 team-member and 65 non-member traders) overestimated significant findings.
limits: One dataset, one mixed-gambles task. A meta-analysis across teams still gave significant consensus in activated regions. Four teams mis-modelled gain against overall task activation.
agent_relevance: A robustness warning: the gain-in-vmPFC effect was not reliably recovered under free analysis. Do not treat one run or one prompt as the result; aggregate across variants.

source: Louie et al. (2014) Dynamic divisive normalization predicts time-varying value coding in decision-related circuits
finding: Value coding in parietal and frontal cortex is context-dependent: firing for an option is scaled by the summed value of alternatives. A dynamic model explains time-varying value coding and reference dependence.
numbers: Empirical test in monkey lateral intraparietal neurons. Model predicts value coding in initial transients and delayed onset of contextual information. No effect sizes extracted.
limits: Parietal data, not vmPFC. A relative rather than absolute common currency.
agent_relevance: Value is relative to the menu. A scaffold that scores options one at a time may show context effects, so rescoring in context is worth a check.

source: Mazeika et al. (2025) Utility Engineering: analyzing and controlling emergent value systems in AIs
finding: Independently sampled pairwise preferences of LLMs fit a Thurstonian utility model, and the fit gets better with scale. The authors read this as emergent value systems.
numbers: 500 textual outcomes, forced-choice pairs, 18 open-source and 5 proprietary LLMs. Figure 4 plots utility-model accuracy against MMLU with correlation 75.6%. Cyclicity (non-transitive preferences) falls as MMLU rises. A citizen-assembly alignment case study reduced political bias.
limits: Coherence of stated forced choices is not proof of an internal common scale. Narrow budget tasks already show rationality (Chen 2023, Raman 2024, Kim 2024, cited there).
agent_relevance: Direct LLM analogue of a common currency: a fitted scalar utility over very different outcomes. Useful as a check that option comparisons are transitive.

source: Chen, Liu, Shan, Zhong (2023) The Emergence of Economic Rationality of GPT
finding: GPT's budget decisions in four domains (risk, time, social, food) nearly satisfy utility maximisation, better than human subjects.
numbers: Average CCEI for GPT 0.998 (risk), 0.997 (time), 0.997 (social), 0.999 (food). Human experiment (347 US subjects): 0.980, 0.985, 0.967, 0.963. Literature CCEI range 0.81 to 0.99, mean 0.918. GPT higher than humans in each domain, p<0.01. 25 decisions per domain. GPT preference parameters were less heterogeneous than humans.
limits: Robust to temperature and demographic prompts. Tests consistency, not whether a scalar value exists inside the network.
agent_relevance: Consistent with a coherent value-like structure, but see the framing result. Test our scaffold with reworded frames.

source: Chen et al. (2023), second finding: framing sensitivity
finding: The high rationality score fell significantly when the price framing changed and when a discrete choice setting was used.
numbers: Stated in the abstract and introduction as drops significantly under different price framing and discrete choice. Exact post-drop CCEI not extracted.
limits: Drop size not recorded here. See the paper's framing section.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: coherence is format-dependent, so check consistency across frames before trusting a model's value scores.

source: Revealed preferences and LLM alignment and steering (2026, medical diagnosis)
finding: Fits discrete-choice cost functions to LLM decisions in four medical diagnosis domains. Models are often internally coherent, but cannot accurately state the costs their choices imply and are hard to steer to a user-given cost ratio.
numbers: Models include DeepSeek, Llama and GPT (high and minimal reasoning). Cost ratios (false negative over false positive, deferral over false positive) estimated under self-report, baseline, true-p and elicited-p prompts. Revealed preferences predicted downstream actions better than stated ones.
limits: Medical diagnosis only. Exact coherence numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Stated values and used values can differ. Our agent should infer trade-offs from behaviour rather than accept a self-report.

source: Alignment revisited: are LLMs consistent in stated and revealed preferences? (2025)
finding: Stated general principles and choices in concrete scenarios often diverge. Small prompt format changes can flip a choice.
numbers: Models: GPT-4.1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Gemini 2.0 Flash. Claude gave neutral answers to general base questions in 84% on average across categories, so it was excluded from the deviation analysis. KL divergence used. GPT said yes in 10 of 11 paraphrases for contribution-based fairness.
limits: Binary forced choice, few models, deviation measured against a self-built prior.
agent_relevance: Different contexts activate different principles. That argues for context-specific scoring and against one global scale.

source: An analysis of AI decision under risk: prospect theory emerges in large language models (2025)
finding: Reasoning and non-reasoning LLMs show gain/loss framing effects in some risky scenarios, but the effect is uneven across contexts and vanishes when scenarios are described in plain mathematics.
numbers: Models: o3, Claude-4, Claude-4-Thinking, GPT-4o, Gemini-1.5-Pro. Championship scenario: loss frame BLITZ chosen 85.6% (107 of 125), gain frame CONTROL chosen 88.8% (111 of 125). Business merger effect not significant for o3 (p=0.3984), significant for Claude-4-Thinking (p=0.0102). Career transition showed a reversed effect in all models. Mann-Whitney U tests.
limits: Self-designed scenarios, three-option format, aggregated models. Limited correlation between doing explicit expected-value calculation and size of the framing effect.
agent_relevance: Valuation in LLMs is frame-dependent, like human reference dependence. A debiasing step should restate options in neutral numeric form.

source: Language models trained to do arithmetic predict human risky and intertemporal choice (2025)
finding: A small GPT trained only on expected-value arithmetic predicts human risky and intertemporal choices better than many cognitive models. Ablating ecological arithmetic data reduces the match.
numbers: R2 for human choices (choices13k, cpc18, gershman20, agrawal23): Arithmetic-GPT ecological 70.8%, 65.5%, 67.8%, 95.5%; ecological ablated 61.4%, 33.8%, 60.7%, 80.1%; untrained 21.0%, 28.4%, 10.8%, 21.1%; LLaMA3 text 14.2%, 8.3%, 4.0%, 3.0%; LLaMA3 text embeddings 66.2%, 55.7%, 66.5%, 98.0%.
limits: Uses embeddings with logistic regression, not generated choices. LLaMA3 matched it on intertemporal choice. Origin of the similarity remains unclear.
agent_relevance: Value-like structure in choice can come from the arithmetic of expected value in training data, not from any brain-like valuation system.

source: Chib, Rangel, Shimojo, O'Doherty (2009) Evidence for a common representation of decision values for dissimilar goods in human vmPFC
finding: Cited in the 2025 review as evidence that vmPFC encodes value for different goods on a shared scale (nonfood consumables and money). Not opened.
numbers: Numbers not read this session.
limits: Only a second-hand description.
agent_relevance: Key founding study to open in a later pass.

source: Levy and Glimcher (2012) The root of all value: a neural common currency for choice
finding: Cited by every review I read as the central statement of the common-currency view. Not opened.
numbers: Numbers not read this session.
limits: Only a second-hand description.
agent_relevance: Open if an exact statement of the claim is needed.

source: Levy, Snell, Nelson, Rustichini, Glimcher (2010) Neural representation of subjective value under risk and ambiguity
finding: Described in the 2025 review: risk and ambiguity attitudes were uncorrelated across people, yet striatum and mPFC value signals were shared across both. Not opened.
numbers: Numbers not read this session.
limits: Only second-hand.
agent_relevance: Supports one scale even when behaviours are not correlated.

source: McClure et al. (2004) Separate neural systems value immediate and delayed monetary rewards
finding: Rival two-system account: immediate rewards recruit VS, mPFC and PCC, delayed rewards recruit lateral PFC and parietal areas. Kable and Glimcher showed value tracks discounted value, challenging it. Not opened.
numbers: Numbers not read this session.
limits: Only second-hand, from the 2025 review.
agent_relevance: A rival account displaced in one paradigm by a single-currency account.

source: Bennett, Niv, Langdon (2021) Value-free reinforcement learning: policy optimization as a minimal model of operant behavior
finding: Cited by the 2026 defence paper and by Hayden and Niv as evidence of value-free policy-gradient learning in humans. Not opened.
numbers: Numbers not read this session.
limits: Only second-hand.
agent_relevance: A rival algorithm that bypasses value estimates.

source: Mazeika et al. (2025) Utility Engineering, transitivity result
finding: The chance of preference cycles (x over y, y over z, z over x) in LLM choices falls as model capability (MMLU) rises. Bigger models are also more decisive in each comparison.
numbers: 500 outcomes; 18 open-source and 5 proprietary LLMs; completeness proxy is average confidence of stated preference.
limits: Completeness and transitivity are proxies, and the paper itself says it is unclear whether preferences are coherent or only look so.
agent_relevance: A cheap check for our agent: rank options pairwise and count cycles. Frequent cycles signal an unreliable value estimate.

source: Bartra et al. (2013), decision vs outcome and primary vs secondary rewards
finding: The paper tests whether the same regions code SV when a decision is made and when an outcome arrives, and for primary vs secondary rewards. Abstract reports positive effects in vmPFC and ventral striatum in both stages and both reward types, with partial overlap across reward categories noted in earlier studies.
numbers: Questions 3 and 4 of four. Earlier studies cited: Chib 2009, Kim 2011, Valentin and O'Doherty 2009 for partial overlap; other work reached different conclusions (text not fully read).
limits: I read the framing and abstract, not every subanalysis table.
agent_relevance: Decision-time and outcome-time value may need separate treatment: scoring plans before acting vs judging results afterwards.
